source.title: ModelDiff: A Framework for Comparing Learning Algorithms
source.authors: Harshay Shah; Sung Min Park; Andrew Ilyas; A. Ma̧dry

record.tranche_reason: Tests how training algorithm choices change image classifiers' confidence under feature transformations, extending algorithm comparison to Living17, Waterbirds and CIFAR-10 feature sensitivities; it does not test the catalog's train-versus-test generalization claims directly.
record.gate_note: Rows capture the paper's own counterfactual feature-transformation results and reported test-accuracy comparisons. Generalization-gap topics in the introduction, related work and citations are not results of this study. The feature transformations are artificial interventions and the reported outcome is class confidence, not test error or generalization gap.
record.test_reason: The study measures feature sensitivity and compares training recipes, but does not test any listed version. Its closest comparison to V5 changes batch size, learning rate and learning-rate schedule together, permits early stopping, and does not report actual training durations. The 93.3% versus 89.5% accuracy difference therefore does not establish a batch-size penalty under fixed epoch budgets.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: ModelDiff compares algorithms through their training-data dependencies, and the three case studies identify feature-level behavioral differences associated with augmentation, pre-training and SGD hyperparameters.
record.recipe_differences: Uses datamodel residuals and PCA to identify distinguishing subpopulations, followed by counterfactual feature transformations; reports class-confidence changes and aggregate test accuracy rather than train-test generalization gaps or the specified interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that transformation intensity widens between-algorithm confidence gaps; Living17 crop scale changes sensitivity; Waterbirds yellow and face transformations show different effects by pre-training; CIFAR-10 patches show different effects by SGD-noise configuration.

fits_no_version.finding: Augmented Living17 models show larger spider-web and polka-dot confidence effects than models trained without augmentation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard data augmentation can amplify specific co-occurrence and texture sensitivities.

fits_no_version.finding: ImageNet pre-training suppresses yellow-patch sensitivity but introduces greater human-face sensitivity on Waterbirds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-training can suppress some spurious feature dependencies while amplifying others.

fits_no_version.finding: The low-SGD-noise recipe produces larger confidence shifts from the selected CIFAR-10 patches.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Joint choices of learning rate, schedule and batch size alter sensitivity to selected visual features.

fits_no_version.finding: Augmentation and ImageNet pre-training improve reported test accuracy in their respective comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: These augmentation and pre-training recipes improve held-out performance on Living17 and Waterbirds.

fits_no_version.finding: CIFAR-10 accuracy is 93.3% with learning rate 0.1, scheduled decay and batch size 256, versus 89.5% with fixed learning rate 0.02 and batch size 1024.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested high-SGD-noise recipe attains better held-out accuracy than the tested low-SGD-noise recipe.

record.problems: The measured feature effects are confidence shifts under artificial transformations, not generalization-gap measurements. No uncertainty estimates are reported for extracted results. The confidence outcomes depend on chosen transformations and intensities; the study's results do not test the claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported additional numerical outcomes were omitted. The paper includes figure sweeps of transformation intensity and crop scale, but specific values beyond those stated in text are figure-only and not reconstructed. It also reports datamodel explained variance and similarity analyses, which do not measure the claim versions' train-test gap outcomes and are not extracted as rows.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected held-out performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under equal epoch budgets and whether recipe adaptations remove a batch-size penalty.
Dropout's effect on held-out error, small-data exceptions, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: A held-out accuracy comparison need not report a train-test gap to bear on V5; the obstacles here are the jointly changed recipe and unverified equal epoch budgets. The study cites original generalization work but does not rely on a listed finding as its methodological tool, so T4 is inappropriate.

versions.untested_parts: Whether the same recipes fit random labels and generalize on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and corresponding test error.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD held-out performance.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance or fixed-epoch generalization gaps.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to train-test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring test accuracy.

relation.reason: Section 4.3 discusses prior findings connecting SGD noise and generalization, but its experiments do not establish a result on the specified versions.

tranche.reason: Feature sensitivity and aggregate accuracies do not test a listed version. The closest comparison changes batch size, learning rate and schedule, with loss-based early stopping and no reported actual durations establishing equal epochs for V5.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. CIFAR-10 recipes use at most 100 epochs with early stopping below loss 0.01; high-noise learning rate halves every 20 epochs, whereas low-noise learning rate is fixed.
